title: Therapist skills (in-session response codes)
description: A coding vocabulary for therapist responses in session, so a transcript turn, a supervision note or a tool response can be labeled. Codes map to MITI 4 and MISC 2.5 behavior codes where those exist (field codes). Not used by formulation slots; used by responding-in-session, alliance and session-structure pages. Group avoid holds unhelpful responses.
sources: Miller-Rollnick-2013 § Ch. 6 Core Interviewing Skills: OARS
Padesky-Kennerley-2023 § The 4-Stage Model of Socratic Dialogue

concepts.label: Open question
concepts.definition: A question that invites an elaborated answer in the client's own words, rather than yes, no, or a single fact.
concepts.client_wording: A question I can answer in my own words, at whatever length I want.
concepts.example: "What has the past week been like for you?"
concepts.coding_note: MITI 4 codes open and closed questions together as Q.

concepts.label: Closed question
concepts.definition: A question that limits the answer to yes or no, a choice between options, or a specific fact such as a number or rating.
concepts.client_wording: A quick question with a short answer, like yes, no, or a number.
concepts.example: "Did you try the breathing exercise this week?"
concepts.coding_note: Rating requests (0 to 100) and risk screening questions are closed questions.

concepts.label: Guided discovery
concepts.definition: The overall CBT process in which questions, summaries and experiments help the client reach new perspectives through their own observation and reasoning.
concepts.client_wording: We work things out together, so I discover answers myself instead of being told.
concepts.example: "How could we find out whether that prediction is true?"
sources: Padesky-Kennerley-2023 § The 4-Stage Model of Socratic Dialogue

concepts.label: Socratic questioning
concepts.definition: Padesky's four-stage dialogue of informational questions, empathic listening, summary and synthesizing questions, aimed at guiding discovery rather than changing the client's mind.
concepts.client_wording: Thoughtful questions that help me look at my situation from new angles.
concepts.example: "What did you notice when you spoke up? ... Putting that together, what does it say about the idea that people will laugh?"
sources: Padesky-1993 § Socratic questioning: changing minds or guiding discovery
Padesky-Kennerley-2023 § The 4-Stage Model of Socratic Dialogue
concepts.coding_note: Use the four stage codes when a transcript allows finer coding.

concepts.label: Socratic informational question
concepts.definition: Stage 1 of Socratic dialogue: concrete questions, within the client's knowledge, that bring overlooked or unnoticed information into awareness.
concepts.client_wording: Questions that help me notice facts I knew but hadn't been paying attention to.
concepts.example: "Have there been times you expected to be rejected and it turned out differently?"
sources: Padesky-1993 § Socratic questioning: changing minds or guiding discovery
Padesky-Kennerley-2023 § The 4-Stage Model of Socratic Dialogue

concepts.label: Empathic listening (Socratic stage)
concepts.definition: Stage 2 of Socratic dialogue: listening closely for the client's meanings, emotional reactions and missing information, and using them to choose the next question.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist really listens to what my answers mean to me before asking more.
concepts.example: The therapist hears the client stress the word "again" and asks, "What does it mean to you that it happened again?"
sources: Padesky-1993 § Socratic questioning: changing minds or guiding discovery
Padesky-Kennerley-2023 § The 4-Stage Model of Socratic Dialogue
concepts.coding_note: A stage code. Code the spoken turn itself as a reflection or question; use this code to mark the dialogue stage.

concepts.label: Socratic summary
concepts.definition: Stage 3 of Socratic dialogue: summarizing, often in writing and in the client's words, the information just gathered, to prepare for synthesis.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist pulls together what I just discovered so I can see it all at once.
concepts.example: "Let me write down what you noticed: two people invited you out this month, and a colleague asked for your advice."
sources: Padesky-1993 § Socratic questioning: changing minds or guiding discovery
Padesky-Kennerley-2023 § The 4-Stage Model of Socratic Dialogue

concepts.label: Synthesizing or analytical question
concepts.definition: Stage 4 of Socratic dialogue: a question asking the client to apply the summarized information to their original belief or concern.
concepts.client_wording: A question that asks what all this new information means for my original worry.
concepts.example: "Looking at this list, how does it fit with the thought that nobody wants you around?"
sources: Padesky-1993 § Socratic questioning: changing minds or guiding discovery
Padesky-Kennerley-2023 § The 4-Stage Model of Socratic Dialogue

concepts.label: Minimal encourager
concepts.definition: A brief sound, word or gesture that signals listening and invites the client to keep going, without adding content.
concepts.client_wording: Small sounds or words, like "mm-hm", that show the therapist is with me.
concepts.example: "Mm-hm." "Go on." "I see."
sources: Ivey-etal-2022 § Ch. 6 Encouraging, Paraphrasing, and Summarizing
concepts.coding_note: MITI 4 does not count these utterances.

concepts.label: Simple reflection
concepts.definition: A statement that gives back what the client said with little or no added meaning or emphasis.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist says back what I said, so I know they heard it.
concepts.example: Client: "I'm tired all the time." Therapist: "You're exhausted."

concepts.label: Complex reflection
concepts.definition: A statement that reflects the client's words with added meaning or emphasis, such as an inferred feeling, meaning or the next unspoken step.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist puts into words what I meant, sometimes a bit more than I said.
concepts.example: Client: "I'm tired all the time." Therapist: "And it's starting to feel like this will never lift."

concepts.label: Double-sided reflection
concepts.definition: A complex reflection capturing both sides of the client's ambivalence, usually joining them with "and" rather than "but".
concepts.client_wording: The therapist shows both sides of how I feel: the part that wants change and the part that doesn't.
concepts.example: "Part of you wants to stop checking, and part of you worries something bad will happen if you do."
sources: Miller-Rollnick-2023 § Ch. 14 Responding to Sustain Talk and Discord

concepts.label: Amplified reflection
concepts.definition: A complex reflection that slightly overstates the client's sustain talk, without sarcasm, so the client can back away from the extreme position.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist says my view a bit more strongly than I did, which makes me rethink it.
concepts.example: Client: "My drinking isn't a problem." Therapist: "There's nothing about it that concerns you at all."
sources: Miller-Rollnick-2023 § Ch. 14 Responding to Sustain Talk and Discord
concepts.coding_note: Delivered with sarcasm or disbelief, it becomes Confront (code ts.arguing).

concepts.label: Reflection of feeling
concepts.definition: A reflection that names the client's emotion, stated or implied, often with its context, to show empathic understanding.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist names the feeling I'm having, sometimes before I've found the word.
concepts.example: "You sound really hurt that she didn't call."
sources: Ivey-etal-2022 § Ch. 7 Observing and Reflecting Feelings: The Heart of Empathic Understanding
Hill-etal-2024 § Skills for Exploring and Experiencing Feelings
concepts.coding_note: MITI and MISC code it SR when the client already named the feeling and CR when the feeling is inferred.

concepts.label: Reflection of meaning
concepts.definition: A complex reflection naming the values, beliefs or personal significance beneath the client's account, beyond its facts and feelings.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist helps me see why this matters so much to me.
concepts.example: "Being a reliable father sounds central to who you want to be."
sources: Ivey-etal-2022 § Ch. 11 Reflection of Meaning and Interpretation/Reframing

concepts.label: Collecting summary
concepts.definition: A summary that gathers several related client statements, often change talk, and offers them back before inviting the client to continue.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist gathers up the things I've said so far and hands them back to me.
concepts.example: "So far you've said you miss your friends, you're sleeping badly, and work feels pointless. What else?"
sources: Miller-Rollnick-2013 § Ch. 6 Core Interviewing Skills: OARS
Ivey-etal-2022 § Ch. 6 Encouraging, Paraphrasing, and Summarizing
concepts.coding_note: MITI 4 and MISC 2.5 code a summary as a reflection, usually complex.

concepts.label: Linking summary
concepts.definition: A summary connecting what the client just said with something said earlier or in a past session, to show a pattern or ambivalence.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist connects what I'm saying now with something I said before.
concepts.example: "That sounds like what happened with your sister last month: you stayed quiet, then felt resentful."
sources: Miller-Rollnick-2013 § Ch. 6 Core Interviewing Skills: OARS

concepts.label: Transitional summary
concepts.definition: A summary that draws together a topic or session segment and signals a shift to a new task or topic.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist wraps up one topic before we move on to the next.
concepts.example: "Let me sum up what we've covered about sleep before we turn to your action plan."
sources: Miller-Rollnick-2013 § Ch. 6 Core Interviewing Skills: OARS

concepts.label: Capsule summary
concepts.definition: A brief CBT summary made at intervals in a session, condensing the main points or conclusion of an agenda item, ideally in the client's words.
concepts.client_wording: A quick recap partway through the session, so we're both clear on what we've worked out.
concepts.example: "So the main thing we found is that the thought 'I'll fail' made you put off starting, and starting small helped."
sources: Blackburn-etal-2001 § Item Pacing and efficient use of time
concepts.coding_note: Distinct from MI summaries: it consolidates CBT learning, often written down for the client.

concepts.label: Affirmation
concepts.definition: A genuine statement recognizing the client's strengths, efforts, intentions or worth, focused on the client rather than on the therapist's approval.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist points out something I did well or a strength I have.
concepts.example: "You came today even though getting out of the house was hard. That took real determination."
concepts.coding_note: Generic praise without a specific client strength or effort ("Great!") is not an affirmation in MITI 4.

concepts.label: Empathic statement
concepts.definition: A compassionate or understanding comment conveying that the therapist grasps and cares how hard something is for the client.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist shows they get how hard this is for me.
concepts.example: "That sounds really painful to go through."
sources: Ivey-etal-2022 § Ch. 3 Listening, Attending and Empathy
concepts.coding_note: If the turn restates client content, code a reflection instead. MITI 4 has no separate code.

concepts.label: Normalizing
concepts.definition: Conveying, with accurate information, that an experience or symptom is common and understandable rather than a sign of being abnormal or broken.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist helps me see that what I'm going through is common, not a sign I'm broken.
concepts.example: "Most people get unwanted, upsetting thoughts popping into their heads. Having them doesn't mean you want them."
concepts.coding_note: Differs from validation level 5: normalizing informs how common an experience is; level 5 validates a specific reaction as reasonable now.

concepts.label: Validation
concepts.definition: Communicating that the client's emotions, thoughts or actions are understandable and make sense, given their history, situation or nature.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist lets me know my reactions make sense.
concepts.example: "Given everything that happened, it makes sense you'd be wary of trusting people."
concepts.coding_note: Validating a response does not mean agreeing it is effective or true. Use a level code when the level is clear.

concepts.label: Validation level 1: attending
concepts.definition: Listening and observing with full, nonjudgmental attention and interest, so the client sees they are taken seriously.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist pays full attention to me without judging.
concepts.example: The therapist sets notes aside, keeps eye contact, and follows up on the detail the client just gave.

concepts.label: Validation level 2: accurate reflection
concepts.definition: Accurately reflecting back the client's own stated feelings, thoughts and assumptions, without judgment, to communicate understanding.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist says back what I feel and think, so I know they understood.
concepts.example: "You felt dismissed when your manager talked over you."
concepts.coding_note: Overlaps with reflection codes. Use when the reflection serves a validating function.

concepts.label: Validation level 3: articulating the unverbalized
concepts.definition: Putting into words feelings, thoughts or meanings the client has not stated, inferred from context or behavior, offered tentatively for correction.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist guesses what I'm feeling but haven't said, and checks if they're right.
concepts.example: "I wonder if part of you also felt embarrassed. Is that close?"

concepts.label: Validation level 4: past learning or biology
alt_labels: validating in terms of sufficient causes
concepts.definition: Conveying that a response makes sense given the client's history, past learning or biology, even if it is not effective now.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist explains why I react this way, given what I've been through.
concepts.example: "After years of being criticized at home, of course you brace yourself for criticism."
sources: Linehan-1997 § Level 4: Validating in terms of past learning or biological dysfunction

concepts.label: Validation level 5: reasonable in the present context
concepts.definition: Conveying that the response is reasonable, normal or effective given the current situation, one most people would share.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist tells me most people would react the same way in my situation.
concepts.example: "Anyone waiting for biopsy results would feel on edge."
sources: Linehan-1997 § Level 5: Validating in terms of present context or normative functioning

concepts.label: Validation level 6: radical genuineness
concepts.definition: Treating the client as a capable equal, not as fragile or merely a patient, and responding genuinely as one person to another.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist treats me as a capable equal and is real with me.
concepts.example: The therapist responds to the client's good news with spontaneous, genuine delight rather than a scripted reflection.

concepts.label: Psychoeducation
concepts.definition: Providing information about a condition, the CBT model or how a problem works, tailored to the client and checked for understanding.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist explains how my problem works in a way I can follow.
concepts.example: "When you leave the supermarket, the anxiety drops fast, which teaches your brain that escaping is what kept you safe."
sources: Beck-2021 § Ch. 6 The First Therapy Session

concepts.label: Giving a rationale
concepts.definition: Explaining why a proposed task, technique or homework should help, linked to the client's formulation and goals, before asking them to try it.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist explains why we're doing something and how it connects to my goals.
concepts.example: "An activity log shows us how what you do links to your mood, so we can pick changes that help."
sources: Eubanks-etal-2019 § Table 1 Resolution strategies (illustrating tasks or providing a rationale)

concepts.label: Asking permission
concepts.definition: Asking the client's consent before offering information, advice, feedback or a sensitive topic, leaving the client free to decline.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist asks if it's okay before sharing advice or raising something sensitive.
concepts.example: "Would it be all right if I shared what other people have found helpful?"
sources: Miller-Rollnick-2023 § Ch. 11 Offering Information and Advice

concepts.label: Elicit-provide-elicit
concepts.definition: An information exchange sequence: ask what the client knows or wants to know, offer information briefly, then ask what they make of it.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist asks what I know, shares a bit, then asks what I think of it.
concepts.example: "What do you already know about how sleep affects mood? ... Studies show ... What do you make of that?"
sources: Miller-Rollnick-2023 § Ch. 11 Offering Information and Advice
concepts.coding_note: A sequence code spanning several turns; code each turn separately when counting MITI behaviors.

concepts.label: Advice with permission
concepts.definition: Offering a suggestion or recommendation after the client asks or agrees, framed so the client remains free to decide.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist offers a suggestion once I've said I want one, and I'm free to choose.
concepts.example: "Since you asked, one option is a fixed wake-up time. You know your life best, so see if it fits."

concepts.label: Emphasizing autonomy
concepts.definition: A statement highlighting the client's choice, control and right to decide about change, without blame.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist reminds me that the choices are mine to make.
concepts.example: "It's your call whether to try this. You know what you're ready for."

concepts.label: Agenda setting
concepts.definition: Collaboratively deciding near the start of a session which topics or problems to cover, in what order, and for roughly how long.
concepts.client_wording: At the start, we agree together on what to talk about today.
concepts.example: "What would you like on today's agenda? I'd also like to review the action plan. Which should we start with?"
sources: Blackburn-etal-2001 § Item Agenda setting and adherence

concepts.label: Eliciting feedback
concepts.definition: Asking the client for reactions to the session, the therapist or a task, including what was unhelpful, and acting on the answer.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist asks what I thought of the session, including what didn't work for me.
concepts.example: "Was there anything I said today that bothered you, or anything we should do differently next time?"

concepts.label: Checking understanding
concepts.definition: Confirming shared understanding: asking the client to restate a key point or plan, or asking whether the therapist's understanding is accurate.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist checks we understand each other, like asking me to put the plan in my own words.
concepts.example: "Just so I know I explained it clearly, how would you describe the plan for this week?"
sources: Ivey-etal-2022 § Ch. 6 Encouraging, Paraphrasing, and Summarizing

concepts.label: Collaborative goal setting
concepts.definition: Working with the client to turn problems into specific, client-owned, measurable goals and agreeing on the tasks to reach them.
concepts.client_wording: We agree together on clear goals for therapy that matter to me.
concepts.example: "If therapy went well, what would you be doing in three months that you aren't doing now?"

concepts.label: Reframing
concepts.definition: Offering a different, plausible meaning for something the client described, which changes its emotional valence, for example from weakness to care.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist offers a new way of looking at something that changes how it feels.
concepts.example: "You call it nagging. It also sounds like how much you care about his health."
sources: Ivey-etal-2022 § Ch. 11 Reflection of Meaning and Interpretation/Reframing
concepts.coding_note: Unlike Socratic questioning, the therapist supplies the new meaning. Offer it tentatively.

concepts.label: Acknowledging the rupture
concepts.definition: Noticing and openly naming a strain in the relationship, such as withdrawal, appeasing or a complaint, instead of ignoring it.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist notices when something feels off between us and says so.
concepts.example: "I notice you've gone quiet since I suggested the exposure task."
sources: Eubanks-etal-2019 § Table 1 Withdrawal and confrontation markers
Eubanks-etal-2018 § Definitions of rupture and repair

concepts.label: Taking responsibility for the rupture
concepts.definition: Acknowledging, without defensiveness, the therapist's own part in a rupture, such as a misunderstanding or pushing too fast.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist owns their part when something they did upset me.
concepts.example: "I think I pushed too quickly there, and that's on me."
sources: Eubanks-etal-2019 § Table 1 Resolution strategies (therapist acknowledges contribution to rupture)

concepts.label: Metacommunication
concepts.definition: Talking about what is happening between client and therapist in the moment, including disclosing the therapist's own experience of the interaction.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist talks openly about what's going on between us right now.
concepts.example: "I'm feeling a bit stuck, as if we're both trying hard but missing each other. Does it feel that way to you?"
sources: Eubanks-etal-2019 § Table 1 Resolution strategies (disclosing internal experience)

concepts.label: Exploring the rupture
concepts.definition: Inviting the client to express negative thoughts and feelings about the therapist or therapy, and staying with them nondefensively.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist invites me to say what I'm unhappy about in therapy, and really listens.
concepts.example: "What was it like when I suggested that? I'd really like to hear, even if it's critical."
sources: Eubanks-etal-2019 § Table 1 Resolution strategies (inviting thoughts or feelings about the therapist or therapy)

concepts.label: Changing the task or goal
concepts.definition: Responding to a rupture by changing, pausing or adjusting the current task or goal so that it better fits the client.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist changes what we're doing when the current approach isn't working for me.
concepts.example: "Let's set the thought record aside today and talk about what's been weighing on you."
sources: Eubanks-etal-2019 § Table 1 Resolution strategies (changing tasks or goals)

concepts.label: Purposeful silence
concepts.definition: Deliberately pausing without speaking to give the client time to think, feel or continue, while remaining visibly attentive.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist gives me quiet time to think or feel before saying more.
concepts.example: After the client says "I've never told anyone that," the therapist stays quietly attentive for several seconds.

concepts.label: Self-disclosure
concepts.definition: Revealing something personal, such as a similar experience or feeling, briefly and for the client's benefit, then returning the focus to the client.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist briefly shares something about themselves that helps me, then turns back to me.
concepts.example: "I've had to work on putting things off too. Starting with five minutes helped me. Could that fit for you?"
sources: Ivey-etal-2022 § Ch. 12 Action Skills for Building Resilience and Managing Stress
concepts.coding_note: Disclosure about the here-and-now relationship is coded ts.repair-metacommunication.

concepts.label: Humor
concepts.definition: Light, well-timed humor attuned to the client and the alliance, used to ease tension or offer perspective, never at the client's expense.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist and I can share a light moment without it making fun of me.
concepts.example: "So your anxiety has been working overtime as your unpaid personal assistant."
sources: Franzini-2001 § Whole article (uses and risks of humor)

concepts.label: Righting reflex
concepts.definition: The urge to fix the client's problem by persuading, advising or arguing for change, which tends to provoke the client's counterarguments.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist jumps in to fix things or tell me what to do before understanding me.
concepts.example: Avoid: "You really need to stop drinking. Have you tried just not buying it?"
sources: Miller-Rollnick-2023 § Ch. 1 The Mind and Heart When Helping

concepts.label: Lecturing
concepts.definition: Extended one-way explanation or information giving without checking the client's knowledge, interest or reaction.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist talks at me for a long time instead of with me.
concepts.example: Avoid: several minutes on sleep hygiene rules with no question to the client.
sources: Miller-Rollnick-2023 § Ch. 11 Offering Information and Advice

concepts.label: Premature reassurance
concepts.definition: Reassuring before understanding the client's concern, or in reply to anxious reassurance seeking, which dismisses feelings and can maintain anxiety.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist says everything will be fine before really hearing my worry.
concepts.example: Avoid: "Don't worry, I'm sure it's nothing serious."

concepts.label: Arguing
concepts.definition: Directly disagreeing, correcting, criticizing or debating with the client in a way that sets the therapist against the client's view.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist argues with me or tells me I'm wrong.
concepts.example: Avoid: "No, that's just not true, and you know it."
concepts.coding_note: Socratic questioning tests beliefs with the client; arguing contests them against the client.

concepts.label: Interrupting
concepts.definition: Cutting into the client's speech or changing topic before they finish, outside brief purposeful redirection, signaling that the therapist's agenda matters more.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist cuts me off before I've finished.
concepts.example: Avoid: "Right, right, but let's get back to the homework" while the client is mid-sentence about a loss.
sources: Ivey-etal-2022 § Ch. 3 Listening, Attending and Empathy
Blackburn-etal-2001 § Item Pacing and efficient use of time

concepts.label: Labeling the client
concepts.definition: Applying a fixed, judgmental label or diagnosis to the client as a person, such as "resistant" or "in denial", instead of describing behavior.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist puts a label on me instead of seeing me as a person.
concepts.example: Avoid: "The problem is that you're in denial."

concepts.label: Premature advice
concepts.definition: Telling the client what to do before understanding the problem or getting permission, often solving the wrong problem.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist tells me what to do before understanding my situation or asking if I want advice.
concepts.example: Avoid: "You should just talk to your boss about it," a minute after hearing the problem.

concepts.label: Tentative hypothesis
concepts.definition: Offering an inference about a thought, belief or pattern as a possibility the client can confirm or correct, never stated as fact.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist shares a guess about what might be going on and asks if it fits.
concepts.example: "I might be off here, so tell me if this doesn't fit. I wonder if 'useless' is the word that keeps coming back."
sources: Young-Beck-1980 § Item 8 Clairvoyance and underlying assumptions
concepts.coding_note: Code a complex reflection when stated, a question when asked. Stating the hypothesis as fact is clairvoyance (avoid).

concepts.label: Instilling hope
concepts.definition: Building realistic expectation of benefit through a credible, personalized rationale, honest answers about likely progress, and visible evidence of change, without promising outcomes.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist helps me see realistic reasons to expect things can improve, without empty promises.
concepts.example: "I can't promise, but this approach helps many people with this problem, and we'll check every few weeks whether it's helping you."
concepts.coding_note: Differs from premature reassurance: hope rests on a rationale the client accepts and on evidence. Assess hopelessness for risk first.

concepts.label: Highlighting progress
concepts.definition: Drawing the client's attention to specific, measured improvement and crediting their own actions for it, so early gains build hope and engagement.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist points out what has improved, with numbers, and what I did to make it happen.
concepts.example: "Two weeks ago you rated the dread at 80. Today it's 55. What did you do differently?"
concepts.coding_note: Crediting the client's effort codes as affirmation; reporting scores alone codes as giving information.

concepts.label: Nonverbal attunement
concepts.definition: Using posture, facial expression, eye contact, pace and tone of voice that fit the client's state and match the therapist's words.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist's face, voice and pace show they are with me and match what they say.
concepts.example: With a tearful client, the therapist slows down, softens their voice and keeps a calm, open posture.
sources: Richmond-etal-2012 § Domain II Do Not Be Provocative
concepts.coding_note: Not a verbal code; note it from observation. A reflection said with a disapproving tone codes as confronting.

concepts.label: Using the client's words
concepts.definition: Repeating the client's own key words, images and metaphors in reflections and summaries instead of translating them into technical terms.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist uses my words and images, not jargon.
concepts.example: "You called it 'the fog'. When the fog comes down, what happens next?"

concepts.label: Plain language
concepts.definition: Explaining ideas in everyday words and short sentences, adding a technical term only after the plain version and only if it helps.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist explains things in everyday words I can follow.
concepts.example: "Thoughts that pop into your head" before "automatic thoughts".

concepts.label: Redirecting to the agenda
concepts.definition: Politely interrupting a peripheral or circular discussion with a brief summary and a link back to the agreed agenda item.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist kindly steers us back to what I said matters most today.
concepts.example: "Can I stop you there for a moment? I want to make sure we get to the panic at work, which you said mattered most today."
sources: Young-Beck-1980 § Item 6 Pacing and Efficient Use of Time
concepts.coding_note: Differs from ts.interrupting (avoid): it is polite, agreed in advance and returns to the client's own priority.

concepts.label: Grounding in session
concepts.definition: Bringing a dissociating or overwhelmed client back to the present by orienting to time and place and directing attention to concrete sensations.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist helps me come back to the here and now by noticing what I can sense.
concepts.example: "Can you feel your feet on the floor? Tell me three things you can see in this room."

concepts.label: Verbal de-escalation
concepts.definition: Responding to anger or agitation with calm, concise speech, respectful distance, honest agreement where possible, clear limits and choices.
concepts.client_wording: When I'm very angry, the therapist stays calm, listens and helps me settle.
concepts.example: "You're really angry, and you have good reason to be upset about the wait. I want to understand. Can we sit down and go through it?"

concepts.label: Asking directly about suicide
concepts.definition: Asking plainly and calmly whether the client is thinking about suicide when hopelessness or distress appears, then assessing risk if indicated.
concepts.client_wording: The therapist asks me straight out about thoughts of suicide, so we can keep me safe.
concepts.example: "Sometimes when people feel this hopeless they think about ending their life. Has that been on your mind?"
concepts.coding_note: Record the answer and the next step taken.
